doc_summary: The paper proposes an 'active' unit test for adversarial robustness evaluations: plant a guaranteed adversarial example in a modified model and check whether the evaluation's attack finds it, flagging weak evaluations in 11 of 13 published defenses. It frames evaluations as proofs whose burden is on the evaluator, and stresses calibrating test difficulty and recognizing the test's blind spots.

items.claim: Prefers actively planting a known ground-truth positive (an injected adversarial example) over passively observing that an attack fails, because failure alone cannot distinguish a robust model from a weak attack.
items.quote: Our test purposefully injects adversarial examples into a defense and then checks if the attack used to evaluate the defense is able to find them. If the attack fails this test, we know that the attack is too weak

items.claim: Prefers treating a null result as uninformative unless the evaluator proves the instrument could have detected the effect, because absence of a finding is ambiguous between true robustness and weak probing.
items.quote: There are two reasons an attack might not find an adversarial example. Either the classifier is robust or the attack is too weak and it could not find the existing adversarials.

items.claim: Calibrate the difficulty of a test against a trivial baseline (random attack) and start from the hardest setting, because a test that is too easy has no predictive power and one too hard underestimates real ability.
items.quote: a test that is too easy has no predictive power about the attack’s efficacy (since any attack might trivially pass it), while on the other hand, a test that is too challenging might actually underestimate the attack’s true performance

items.claim: Prefers framing evaluations as proofs with the null hypothesis that the claim is false, putting the burden on the evaluator to give convincing evidence rather than on critics to produce a counterexample.
items.quote: This is because the null hypothesis for a theorem is that it is false, just as the null hypothesis for a defense should be that it is not robust.

items.claim: Distrusts evaluations whose attack ignores the component being claimed as a defense (e.g., oblivious to the detector), so the paper adds an inverted test so that passing a single direction cannot mask this.
items.quote: a potential issue with the regular test is that a weak attack might pass the test even though the attack completely ignores the detector. Indeed, many evaluations of detector defenses consider weak attacks that are oblivious

items.claim: When a check passes but the evaluation is known to be broken, diagnose it as a different class of bug (integration vs unit) rather than discarding the test; be explicit about what the test cannot catch.
items.quote: If we view our proposed test as a unit test for an attack, then the type of bug in the above evaluation is akin to an integration bug, where the (correct) attack is called with incorrect parameters.

items.claim: Claims a test is a necessary but not sufficient condition, and that a failed test undermines confidence without proving the defense is broken, because over-claiming from a one-sided check is unjustified.
items.quote: Note that this does not necessarily imply that the theorem is not correct (a.k.a. that the defense is not effective), but it should not give us any confidence that it is.

items.claim: Validate a new diagnostic against cases with known ground truth (previously broken defenses with weak vs strong attacks), reporting true/false positives, rather than only demonstrating it on fresh cases.
items.quote: we now have access to both a flawed and a well-working adversarial evaluation method for each defense. This allows us to compare how these attacks perform in terms of both the estimated robust accuracy and the score on the binarization test.

items.claim: Suggests that each defense author should build tailored attack unit tests matched to their particular claims and architecture rather than relying on one generic test.
items.quote: defense authors should aim to develop their own attack unit tests, depending on the particular claims made.

items.claim: Treats concrete code-level flaws found in the evaluation (e.g., unfrozen batch norm) as the decisive confirmation that a low test score reflects a real weakness, and checks by fixing and re-testing.
items.quote: Upon investigation, we found a flaw in the original evaluation’s code: The statistics of the batch normalization layers are not frozen during evaluation, which changes the behavior of the model during the attack.
